title: Chanthaburi Nature Trip: 3 Days of Waterfalls & Sea | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A 3-day, 2-night nature itinerary for Chanthaburi, Thailand: Phlio Waterfall, Khao Khitchakut, and the Tung Prong Thong mangrove boardwalk. Hour-by-hour timing, real entry fees, the best season to go, and a backup plan if Khao Khitchakut is closed.
keywords: Chanthaburi nature itinerary, Phlio Waterfall, Khao Khitchakut, Tung Prong Thong, Kung Krabaen Bay, Chaloem Burapha Chonlathit coastal road
h1:
A Nature Itinerary for Chanthaburi
Waterfall, Mountain & Mangrove in 3 Days
intro: Chanthaburi packs a lot of nature into a short drive — a waterfall that runs all year, a pilgrimage mountain that only opens in the dry season, and mangrove forest along the eastern coast. This plan spreads it over 3 days and 2 nights, starting at Phlio Waterfall, climbing Khao Khitchakut, then finishing on the coastal road with a wooden boardwalk through the mangroves. Real timings, real entry fees, and backup options all the way through.

blocks.html: Before we start, two honest things set this plan apart. First, Khao Khitchakut only opens during the Buddha Footprint pilgrimage festival, roughly mid-January to mid-March (the most recent run was about Jan 19 – Mar 19). Outside that window the mountain is closed and you simply can't climb it. Second, the Tung Prong Thong boardwalk that everyone pictures is actually at Pak Nam Prasae, Klaeng District, in Rayong province — not in Chanthaburi at all. But it sits on the same coastal road and is only about an hour's drive on from Chanthaburi, so it slots easily into the trip. If you'd rather not leave the province, we've got a Chanthaburi mangrove walk to use instead.

blocks.text: Trip overview and when to go

blocks.html: A car makes this plan far easier, because the stops are scattered in different directions. Phlio Waterfall and Khao Khitchakut are inland, while the mangroves and viewpoints are on the coast. Drive times between stops are mostly 30–60 minutes. Book accommodation in two zones: night one in Chanthaburi town, and night two around Chao Lao Beach and Kung Wiman to end the trip by the sea.

items: The sweet spot — January to March: cool weather, the waterfall still has water, and it's the only stretch when Khao Khitchakut is open.
Rainy season (May–Oct) — Phlio Waterfall runs full and green, but Khao Khitchakut is closed, so swap in the mangroves and the coast instead.
Avoid long weekends — when Khao Khitchakut is open, tens of thousands climb per day and the songthaew queues get long. A weekday is far more comfortable.

blocks.title: Check this before you set off
blocks.html: Khao Khitchakut's open and close dates shift every year with the lunar calendar. Always check the announcement from TAT Chanthaburi or Wat Phluang first. If you're going outside the festival window, just skip Day 2 and head straight to the coast.

blocks.title: Book the activities in your Chanthaburi trip ahead
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

items.label: Day trips from Chanthaburi
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.text: Day 1 — Phlio Waterfall and into town

blocks.html: Take the first day easy with a half-day at Phlio Waterfall, which flows year-round. It's a short, gently sloping walk from the car park, manageable for kids and adults alike. The highlight is a clear pool full of soro brook carp, plus two old monuments inside the falls grounds: the Alongkorn Pyramid and the memorial King Rama V built in honour of Queen Sunanda Kumariratana.

items.activity: Arrive at Namtok Phlio National Park, buy your entry ticket
items.note: Thai adults 40 THB, children 20 THB. Open roughly 08:00–17:00 daily.

items.activity: Walk up to the main falls, watch the soro brook carp in the clear pool, stop at the Alongkorn Pyramid
items.note: Shady path, gentle slope — wear comfortable walking shoes.

items.activity: Leave the falls, find lunch around Laem Sing District or on the way into town
Check in to your town accommodation, stroll the Chanthaboon Riverside Community
items.note: An old riverside community with vintage wooden houses, the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, and small cafés.

items.activity: Dinner of Chanthaburi specialties — crab-fried sen chan noodles or moo liang noodle soup
items.note: Walk back to sleep in town so you're ready for the early climb the next morning.

blocks.html: If your dates fall within the festival, this is the pilgrimage highlight. Khao Khitchakut — also called Phra Bat Phluang — is a sacred Buddha footprint on a peak around 1,000 metres up. The route is very steep: you ride locals' songthaews up in stages, then walk several more kilometres on foot to reach the top. Many people climb in the dead of night to catch the morning light on the summit. Expect it to be genuinely tiring and genuinely crowded, but the atmosphere up top with the sea of morning mist is worth the effort.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Climb Khao Khitchakut for the morning light

items.activity: Wake up, leave your accommodation, drive to the Wat Phluang car park and catch a songthaew up the mountain
items.note: Songthaew fare is roughly 100–200 THB per person round trip, paid in stages. Long queues on holidays.

items.activity: Walk the final stretch to the summit and pay respects at the Buddha footprint
items.note: Steep path with handrails in places. Wear non-slip shoes, carry water and a torch.

items.activity: Catch the morning light on the summit, tie a red cloth as tradition holds, photograph the sea of mist
items.note: It's cold up there — bring a light jacket.

items.activity: Head down, return to town for a late breakfast and a rest
items.note: The descent is hard on the legs, so leave time to recover.

items.activity: Move to the Chao Lao Beach – Kung Wiman zone to set up for the seaside finish

blocks.title: If you're going outside Khao Khitchakut's open season
blocks.html: Use Day 2 as a full beach day instead. Drive the Chaloem Burapha Chonlathit coastal road from Chao Lao Beach all the way to Kung Wiman, stop at the Noen Nang Phaya viewpoint for photos, then swim at Kung Wiman Beach, which is quieter and clearer.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Mangroves and the coastal road

blocks.html: The last day is all coastal nature, with two options for the mangroves. If you want the Tung Prong Thong wooden boardwalk you've seen in photos, drive on into Rayong province for about another hour to Pak Nam Prasae, Klaeng District — a boardwalk stretching roughly 2 km through golden-green mangroves, free to enter. But if you'd rather stay inside Chanthaburi, the province has its own mangrove nature trail at the Kung Krabaen Bay Royal Development Study Center, a boardwalk about 1.6 km long that's also free and much closer.

items.activity: Walk the mangrove boardwalk in the morning, before the sun gets harsh
items.note: Pick Kung Krabaen Bay (Chanthaburi, closer) or Tung Prong Thong at Pak Nam Prasae (Rayong, more photogenic) — both open early and are free to enter.

items.activity: Stop at the Noen Nang Phaya viewpoint on the Chaloem Burapha Chonlathit road to photograph the curving coastal highway
items.note: A long coastal road on the eastern shore — sweeping curves and deep-blue sea.

items.activity: Seafood lunch on Chao Lao Beach or around Kung Krabaen
items.note: This area has fresh oysters and seafood from local farms.

items.activity: Capture Kung Wiman Beach in the afternoon, then start the drive home
items.note: If you have time to spare, waiting for the evening light at Noen Nang Phaya before heading back is worth it.

items: Phlio Waterfall entry — Thai adults 40 THB (children 20 THB)
Khao Khitchakut — free to climb; songthaew round trip roughly 100–200 THB
Mangroves — both Tung Prong Thong and Kung Krabaen Bay are free to enter
2 nights' accommodation — from around 600–1,500 THB per night, depending on whether you stay in town or by the sea
Food — roughly 80–250 THB per meal; seaside seafood runs a little higher

blocks.text: Food worth stopping for along the way

blocks.html: A nature trip doesn't mean missing out on good food — Chanthaburi is a food town. Worth seeking out: crab-fried sen chan noodles, made with the chewy local rice noodle; the rounded, mellow moo liang noodle soup; and fresh oysters around Kung Krabaen. For things to take home, there's Chanthaburi peppercorn and seasonal fruit. If you come during durian season from April to June, the orchards around town open for all-you-can-eat buffet tastings too.

faq.q: Is Khao Khitchakut open all year?
faq.a: No. Khao Khitchakut only opens during the Buddha Footprint pilgrimage festival, roughly mid-January to mid-March each year (the most recent run was about Jan 19 – Mar 19). Outside that window it's closed and you can't climb it. Check the announcement from TAT Chanthaburi or Wat Phluang before you plan.

faq.q: Is Tung Prong Thong in Chanthaburi or Rayong?
faq.a: The Tung Prong Thong boardwalk that everyone has in mind is at Pak Nam Prasae, Klaeng District, in Rayong province — not in Chanthaburi. But it sits on the same coastal road and is only about an hour's drive on from Chanthaburi. If you'd rather not leave the province, Chanthaburi has the Kung Krabaen Bay mangrove walk to use instead.

faq.q: How much does Phlio Waterfall cost, and does it have water year-round?
faq.a: Thai adults 40 THB, children 20 THB, open roughly 08:00–17:00 daily. Phlio Waterfall flows year-round, with more water and an especially lush green look in the rainy season. There's also a school of soro brook carp in the pool to watch.

faq.q: How many days does this nature trip really need?
faq.a: 3 days and 2 nights is just right: day one for Phlio Waterfall and the town, day two for Khao Khitchakut or the sea, day three for the mangroves and the coastal road. If you only have 2 days, cut Khao Khitchakut and focus on the waterfall and the coast instead.

faq.q: Do I need my own car?
faq.a: We'd recommend your own car or a rental, because the stops are scattered in different directions — both inland and coastal. Public transport between these points isn't convenient. If you don't want to drive, you could hire a car with a driver by the day instead.
